answer: With an unknown number of parts, no count-based completeness condition exists, so the consumer or aggregate cannot decide from a count that the split has finished. Spring Integration's base splitter sets SEQUENCE_SIZE to zero for an iterator of unknown size and states that the aggregate group remains incomplete, directing a custom release strategy or send-partial-result-on-expiry. Without an owned release or expiry rule the split either never completes or leaks orphaned work; a declared rule releases a partial result or forces closure instead of reporting silent success. A release or expiry is not evidence of successful completion — it yields a partial result or forced closure, and only a known total part count makes completion decidable — so a partial result needs a caller-visible completeness marker. Camel's value-based watermark advances only when the split completes successfully, leaving an aborted split retryable and requiring idempotent or deduplicated effects. The decision therefore requires an observable outcome and bounded fan-out, each part carrying a correlation identity and sequence position; the rule also trades early release against holding state, and no default timeout is prescribed. If completion cannot be owned, keep the composite whole.
